title: 論語 先進第十一
source: Confucius 孔子 and his disciples, 論語 (the Analects), book 11, 〈先進〉, in the received text as printed in Zhu Xi 朱熹, 論語集注 (part of his 四書章句集注, completed c. 1190), from the Wenyuange 文淵閣 copy of the Siku Quanshu 四庫全書 (1782), as transcribed by the Kanseki Repository (Kanripo, KR1h0015). Collated character by character against two further pre-1930 printings, both transcribed by Kanripo: Ruan Yuan's 1816 Nanchang reprint of the Song edition of 論語注疏 (KR1h0004) and He Yan's 論語集解 in the Sibu Congkan photographic reprint of a Song edition (KR1h0005). Readings that change the sense are noted in the notes; graphic variants (悌 for 弟, 爲 for 為) are not. Zhu Xi's text is substantially the one James Legge printed in The Chinese Classics, vol. 1 (Hong Kong, 1861), and the passage numbering is the standard one. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none. Characters are traditional, as the edition prints them (衆, not 眾). Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Any prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same modern Mandarin convention; the exact voice used is recorded in audio/<id>/voice.txt and is fixed for every Chinese text.
about: Book 11 of the Analects, 先進 Xiān jìn, named, as every book is, from its first words ("Those who came first…"). The Analects is a collection of short sayings and exchanges of Confucius (Kǒngzǐ, 551–479 BC) and his disciples, put together by their followers over several generations; the twenty books were not composed as a whole, and nothing in them was written down by Confucius himself. Zhu Xi's heading says this book mostly weighs the disciples, their strengths and their failings, and it is the book in which they are most alive: the list of ten in four fields — conduct, speech, government, letters (11.2); the Master's sharp words to Zilu (11.14, 11.24) and about Ran You, who was gathering in taxes for the over-rich Ji family (11.16); the one who goes too far and the one who falls short (11.15); the same question given opposite answers by two disciples of opposite temper (11.21). At the centre stands the death of Yan Yuan, the disciple he loved best, told in five short scenes (11.7–11.11), with the Master's cry that Heaven had destroyed him. Zhu Xi quotes Hu Yin's guess that the book, which speaks of Min Ziqian four times and once calls him 'Master Min', may have been set down by Min's own followers. It ends with the longest passage in the book (11.25): four disciples sitting with the Master are asked what they would do if a ruler employed them, and the last of them, who has been playing the zither, answers with a spring outing by the river. Each numbered passage begins a new card; longer passages are cut where Zhu Xi's commentary interrupts the text. The original has no punctuation: every comma, quotation mark and full stop is an editor's interpretation. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
先進於禮樂，
野人也；
後進於禮樂，
君子也。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
The Master said: “Those who came forward first in the rites and music —
men of the countryside;
those who came forward later in the rites and music —
gentlemen.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “The men of the earlier generation, in the rites and music, are counted rustics; the men of the later one are counted gentlemen.”
sentences.n: The book is named 先進 from its opening words. Zhu Xi's heading: much of it weighs the disciples, worthy or not, in twenty-five chapters (He Yan counts twenty-three); he quotes Hu Yin: four passages record Min Ziqian's words and deeds, and one of them calls him simply 'Master Min' (閔子, 11.12), so perhaps Min's own followers wrote it down. The two halves of this line are the same sentence twice: a topic ('those who came forward first in the rites and music'), then a noun predicate closed by 也 — 'X, (they are) Y'. 於 is 'in, in respect of'. 樂 is yuè 'music' here; 禮樂 'the rites and music' together are the whole of cultivated form. Zhu Xi: 先進 and 後進 are 'the earlier and the later generation' (前輩後輩); 野人 are the people out beyond the city walls, 君子 worthy officers and grandees. On his reading the Master is reporting how people of his day talk. He quotes Master Cheng: the earlier men had pattern and substance in due measure in the rites and music, yet people now call them plain and rustic; the later men's pattern outruns their substance, yet people now call them polished, gentlemen — at the end of the Zhou pattern had the upper hand, so men spoke so without seeing their own excess. He Yan's commentary takes the two verdicts more at face value: 先進 and 後進 are earlier and later generations of officers; the rites and music change with the age; the later men have the mean that suits their time, and so are gentlemen, while the earlier keep the old manner, and so are rustics.

sentences.t:
如用之，
則吾從先進。
sentences.l:
If I were to use them,
then I would follow those who came forward first.
sentences.i: But if it were for me to put them to use, I would go with the earlier men.
sentences.n: 如 'if' opens a condition and 則 'then' answers it: the frame you will meet everywhere. 用之 'use them' — Zhu Xi: use the rites and music. 從 cóng 'to follow, go with'. The speech runs on past Zhu Xi's comment; this continuation is left unquoted. Zhu Xi: having given what people of the day said, the Master states where he himself stands, wishing to cut back what is excessive and come to the mean. He Yan's Bao Xian: he would change the customs of the age and bring them back to plainness; and the commentary adds that the earlier men were nearer the old ways, so he followed them.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
從我於陳、蔡者，
皆不及門也。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Those who followed me in Chen and Cai,
all of them, do not reach my gate.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “The men who went through Chen and Cai with me — not one of them is at my door now.”
sentences.n: 陳 Chen and 蔡 Cai were small states south of Lu, where, tradition says, the Master and his followers were cut off and ran short of food. 從我…者 'the ones who followed me…': 者 closes the whole phrase into a noun. Zhu Xi marks this 從 去聲, the reading (zòng) for going along as an attendant; modern practice reads cóng, and so do we here and in 11.9. 皆 'all, without exception'. 不及門 'do not reach the gate'. Zhu Xi: the Master was once in straits between Chen and Cai, and many disciples were with him; now none of them was at his gate, so he thought of them — he did not forget those who had shared his hardship. He Yan's Zheng Xuan reads it another way: those who followed him in his straits all failed to reach 'the gate of office' (仕進之門) and missed their due place. Variant: He Yan's text reads 皆不及門者也, 'were all ones who did not reach the gate'.

政事：冉有、季路。
文學：子游、子夏。

sentences.l:
Virtuous conduct: Yan Yuan, Min Ziqian, Ran Bo Niu, Zhonggong.
Speech: Zai Wo, Zigong.
The affairs of government: Ran You, Ji Lu.
Letters and learning: Ziyou, Zixia.
sentences.i: For virtuous conduct there were Yan Yuan, Min Ziqian, Ran Bo Niu and Zhonggong; for speaking, Zai Wo and Zigong; for the business of government, Ran You and Ji Lu; for letters and learning, Ziyou and Zixia.
sentences.n: A bare list: each heading names a field, then the men who excelled in it. 行 is 'conduct' here; Zhu Xi marks it 去聲 (xìng, the noun), but modern practice reads xíng and so do we. 語 yǔ 'words'. The ten are familiar from earlier books: Yan Yuan is Yan Hui; Min Ziqian is Min Sun (6.7); Ran Bo Niu is Ran Geng, the Bo Niu of 6.8; Zhonggong is Ran Yong; Zai Wo is Zai Yu; Zigong is Duanmu Ci; Ran You is Ran Qiu; Ji Lu is Zilu, Zhong You; Ziyou is Yan Yan; Zixia is Bu Shang. 文學 is not 'literature' in the modern sense but letters and learning: knowledge of the Odes, the Documents and the rites. Zhu Xi: the disciples, prompted by the Master's words above, recorded these ten and listed each one's strength under four heads (the 'four branches', 四科) — which shows the Master taught each man according to his gifts. He quotes Master Cheng: the four branches name only those who were with the Master in Chen and Cai; the worthy disciples were far more than these — Master Zeng, who handed on the Way, is not among them — so the talk of 'the ten wise ones' (十哲) is a popular notion. Variant: He Yan's text puts 子曰 'the Master said' before the list, making it the Master's own words rather than the recorders'.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
回也，
非助我者也，
於吾言無所不說。」
sentences.i: The Master said: “Hui does nothing to help me along. Whatever I say, it all pleases him.”
sentences.n: 回也 'Hui —': a name plus 也 sets up the topic. 非…者也 'is not one who…'. 於吾言 'with respect to my words'. 無所不說 'there is nothing that he is not pleased with': a double negative, 'everything pleases him'. 說 is yuè 'pleased' (Zhu Xi: 音悅). Zhu Xi: 'helping me' is what Zixia did in 3.8 ('the one who stirs me up is Shang') — by doubts and questions teacher and pupil grow together; Yan Hui took in the sage's words silently and understood them in his heart, with nothing to ask, so the Master spoke thus. The words sound almost regretful, but in truth he is deeply pleased. Hu Yin: did the Master really look to Hui for help? It is the sage's modesty, and deep praise of Yan Hui besides. He Yan's Kong Anguo: 助 is 'to add to'; Hui understood as soon as he heard, so there was nothing to set the Master off or add to his thought (無可發起增益).

sentences.t:
子曰：「
孝哉，閔子騫！
人不閒於其父母昆弟之言。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
The Master said: “How filial he is, Min Ziqian!
Others set nothing against the words of his father, mother and brothers.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “What a good son Min Ziqian is! When his parents and brothers speak well of him, no one else has a word to say against it.”
sentences.n: 孝哉閔子騫 puts the predicate first for an exclamation, 'filial — how! — Min Ziqian' (as 9.2 大哉孔子). 閒 jiàn (Zhu Xi: 去聲) is 'a gap', and as a verb 'to find a gap in, to set against': others find no gap between what they say of him and what his own family says. 昆 is an elder brother; 昆弟 'brothers'. Zhu Xi quotes Hu Yin: his parents and brothers praised his filial and brotherly conduct, and everyone believed them, with no word to the contrary; for the reality of it had built up within and showed without, and so the Master sighed and praised him. Min Ziqian is the disciple Min Sun (6.7).

sentences.t:
南容三復白圭，
孔子以其兄之子妻之。

morph.gloss: Rong (in 南容, from his courtesy name Zirong)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Nan Rong three times went over the white jade tablet;
Kongzi gave him his elder brother's daughter as wife.
sentences.i: Nan Rong would repeat the lines about the white jade tablet three times over, and Kongzi gave him his elder brother's daughter in marriage.
sentences.n: Nan Rong is the disciple of 5.1, and the second half of the line repeats 5.1 word for word: 以其兄之子妻之 'taking his elder brother's child, he gave her to him as wife', with 妻 read qì, the verb (Zhu Xi: 去聲). Zhu Xi also marks 三 去聲, a reading for 'over and over'; we print sān, as at 5.19. 白圭 points to an ode in the Major Elegantiae (大雅, the ode 抑), which Zhu Xi quotes: 'A flaw in a white jade tablet can still be ground away; a flaw in these words cannot be mended.' Nan Rong, he says, repeated these lines three times a day (the story is in the Kongzi jiayu) — his heart was set on care in speech, which is why, as 5.1 says, he would not be passed over in a well-governed state nor come to harm in a badly governed one; and so Kongzi gave him his brother's daughter. He quotes Fan Zuyu: words are the outward show of conduct and conduct the substance of words; no one who speaks lightly is careful in what he does, and one so careful of his words must be careful in his deeds too.

sentences.t:
季康子問：「
弟子孰為好學？」
孔子對曰：「
有顔回者好學，
不幸短命死矣，
今也則亡。」

sentences.l:
Ji Kangzi asked: “Of your disciples, who is fond of learning?”
Kongzi answered, saying: “There was Yan Hui, who was fond of learning;
unluckily he was short-lived, and he has died.
Now there is none.”
sentences.i: Ji Kangzi asked which of the disciples loved learning. Kongzi answered: “There was Yan Hui. He loved learning. Sadly he was not given long, and he is dead. Now there is no one.”
sentences.n: Duke Ai asked the same question in the same words in 6.2, and the answer here is that one shortened: it leaves out 'he did not shift his anger, he did not repeat a fault' and the closing 'I have not heard of one fond of learning'. 季康子 Ji Kangzi, head of the Ji house (2.20), is the asker. 孰為好學 'who is fond of learning', 為 wéi 'is', 好 hào (Zhu Xi: 去聲). 亡 is wú, the same word as 無. Zhu Xi quotes Fan Zuyu on why the answers differ in fullness: a minister answering his ruler must tell him everything; one like Kangzi must wait until he can ask properly, and only then be told — this is the way of teaching. Variant: He Yan's text gives the answer at the full length of 6.2 (不遷怒，不貳過 … 未聞好學者也).

sentences.t:
顔淵死，
顔路請子之車以為之椁。

morph.gloss: = 顏 (the edition's form): Yan (a surname, in 顔淵)
Yuan (in 顏淵, from the courtesy name Ziyuan)

sentences.l:
Yan Yuan died;
Yan Lu asked for the Master's carriage, to make an outer coffin for him.
sentences.i: When Yan Yuan died, his father Yan Lu asked for the Master's carriage, so that he could provide an outer coffin for his son.
sentences.n: Zhu Xi: Yan Lu was Yan Yuan's father, personal name Wuyou 無繇; he was six years younger than Confucius and studied with him when the Master first began to teach. 椁 guǒ (the edition's form of 槨) is the outer coffin, the wooden casing set round the coffin itself. 以為之椁 'thereby to make him an outer coffin': 以 'so as to', 為 wéi 'to make', 之 'for him'. Zhu Xi: he asked for the carriage meaning to sell it and buy the outer coffin; He Yan's Kong Anguo says the same, adding that the family was poor. Variant: He Yan's text lacks 以為之椁 — Yan Lu simply 'asked for the Master's carriage'.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
才不才，
亦各言其子也。
鯉也死，
有棺而無椁。
吾不徒行以為之椁。
以吾從大夫之後，
不可徒行也。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Talented or not talented,
each still speaks of his own son.
When Li died,
there was a coffin and no outer coffin.
I did not go on foot to make him an outer coffin.
Because I follow at the rear of the grandees,
I may not go on foot.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Gifted or not, each of us is speaking of his own son. When Li died he had a coffin but no outer coffin; I did not take to walking to give him one. I still have a place, at the back, among the grandees, and it would not do for me to go about on foot.”
sentences.n: 才不才 'talented, not talented' — whether a son is gifted or not. 亦 'still, all the same'. 鯉 Li is Kong Li, the Master's son, courtesy name Boyu, who died before his father (Zhu Xi; He Yan's Kong Anguo). 有棺而無椁 'there was a coffin but no outer coffin'. 徒行 'to go on foot', 徒 tú 'on foot'. 以吾從大夫之後 'because I follow at the rear of the grandees': 以 'because'. Zhu Xi: Li's gifts did not match Yan Yuan's, but to the Master and to Yan Lu, each looking as a father, both were sons. The Master had by then retired from office, but still took his place in the ranks of the grandees; 'at the rear' is modest. He quotes Hu Yin at length: the Master once unharnessed an outside horse as a funeral gift to a former host (a story in the Book of Rites) — why refuse Yan Lu now? A burial can do without an outer coffin, and a horse can be given away and bought again; but a grandee may not go on foot, and the carriage his ruler conferred may not be given to another to be sold in the market; besides, straining to meet the wishes of a poor acquaintance would be neither sincere nor straight. Some say a gentleman performs the rites as his means allow; but the gentleman spends according to what is right, not merely according to what he has. Variants: He Yan's text reads 鯉死 (without 也), 吾不可徒行 'I could not go on foot', and 以吾從大夫之後，吾以不可徒行也.

sentences.t:
顔淵死。
子曰：「
噫！
天喪予！
天喪予！」

morph.gloss: = 顏 (the edition's form): Yan (a surname, in 顔淵)
Yuan (in 顏淵, from the courtesy name Ziyuan)

sentences.l:
Yan Yuan died.
The Master said: “Ah!
Heaven has undone me!
Heaven has undone me!”
sentences.i: When Yan Yuan died, the Master said: “Oh! Heaven has undone me! Heaven has undone me!”
sentences.n: 噫 yī is a cry of grief (Zhu Xi: 傷痛聲; He Yan's Bao Xian: 痛傷之聲). 喪 is sàng 'to destroy, to lose' (Zhu Xi: 去聲), not sāng 'mourning'; 予 yú 'me'. Zhu Xi: he grieved that the Way would have no one to hand it on to, as though Heaven had destroyed him himself. He Yan's commentary: it is as if he himself were lost; he says it twice because his grief is so deep.

sentences.t:
顔淵死，
子哭之慟。
從者曰：「
子慟矣！」

morph.gloss: = 顏 (the edition's form): Yan (a surname, in 顔淵)
Yuan (in 顏淵, from the courtesy name Ziyuan)

sentences.i: When Yan Yuan died, the Master wept for him with a grief that knew no bounds. The disciples with him said: “Master, you are letting grief carry you too far!”
sentences.n: 哭 is the ritual wailing for the dead. 慟 tòng is grief that goes past its proper measure (Zhu Xi and He Yan's Ma Rong: 哀過也); 哭之慟 'wailed for him, overflowing'. 從者 'those following', the disciples with him: Zhu Xi again marks 從 去聲; we read cóng (see 11.2). 子 here is 'you, Master', in address. 矣 marks the state reached: 'you have come to grieve past measure.'

sentences.t:
曰：「
有慟乎？」
sentences.l: He said: “Is it beyond measure?”
sentences.i: “Am I grieving past measure?” he said.
sentences.n: The speaker is the Master (He Yan's text writes 子曰). 有慟乎 'is there grief beyond measure?' Zhu Xi: grief at its height does not know itself. He Yan's Kong Anguo: he did not know that his own grief had gone too far.

sentences.t:
非夫人之為慟，
而誰為？
sentences.l:
If not for that man I grieve thus,
then for whom?
sentences.i: This is the man to grieve for past all measure — who else, if not he?
sentences.n: The Master's reply runs on past Zhu Xi's comment and is left unquoted. 夫 is fú 'that' (Zhu Xi: 音扶), and 夫人 here is 'that man', Yan Yuan — not fūrén 'wife'. 為 is wèi 'for' both times (Zhu Xi: 去聲). The shape 非A而B is 'if not A, then B'. Inside it two objects come first: 夫人之為慟 is 為夫人慟 'grieve for that man' with the object moved ahead and marked by 之, and 誰為 'for whom' puts the question word before its verb, as question words do. Zhu Xi: his death is truly to be mourned, and it is fitting to wail for him past measure — he is not to be compared with others. He quotes Hu Yin: grief at its utmost, yet spent where it was due — all of this is feeling and nature in their right state. Variant: He Yan's text ends 而誰為慟, 'for whom grieve beyond measure?'

sentences.t:
顔淵死，
門人欲厚𦵏之。
子曰：「不可。」

morph.gloss: = 顏 (the edition's form): Yan (a surname, in 顔淵)
Yuan (in 顏淵, from the courtesy name Ziyuan)

sentences.i: When Yan Yuan died, the disciples wanted to give him a grand burial. The Master said: “No, that will not do.”
sentences.n: 門人 'the men of the gate', the Master's disciples. 厚𦵏 'to bury generously' (𦵏 is the edition's form of 葬 zàng). 不可 'not possible, not acceptable'. Zhu Xi: funeral goods should match what the family has; a lavish burial from a poor house does not follow principle, so the Master stopped them. He Yan's commentary says the same: the rites suit rich and poor to their means, and Yan Yuan's family was poor.

sentences.t: 門人厚𦵏之。
sentences.l: The disciples buried him lavishly.
sentences.i: The disciples buried him in grand style all the same.
sentences.n: Zhu Xi: it was probably Yan Lu, the father, who let them do it.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
回也視予猶父也，
予不得視猶子也。
非我也，
夫二三子也。」
sentences.i: The Master said: “Hui regarded me as his father, but I was not permitted to do for him what a father does for a son. I did not choose this — you did, my friends.”
sentences.n: 視…猶… 'to look on … as …'. 予 yú 'I, me'. 不得 'did not get to, was not allowed to'. 夫 fú 'those' (as 11.9), with 二三子 'you two or three', the friendly address to disciples. Zhu Xi: he sighs that he could not bury Hui fittingly as he had buried his son Li (11.7), and so rebukes the disciples. He Yan's Ma Rong: Hui had his own father, and the father wanted to let the disciples bury him lavishly; I could not stop it.

sentences.t:
季路問事鬼神。
子曰：「
未能事人，
焉能事鬼？」「敢問死。」
曰：「
未知生，
焉知死？」

morph.gloss: Ji, the clan name (Jisun) of the Lu house
the spirits — of the dead and of the gods

sentences.l:
Ji Lu asked about serving the spirits of the dead and the gods.
The Master said: “Not yet able to serve men —
how could you serve the dead?” “I venture to ask about death.”
He said: “Not yet understanding life —
how could you understand death?”
sentences.i: Ji Lu asked how one should serve the spirits. The Master said: “Serving the living is still beyond you; how would you go about serving the dead?” “And may I ask about death?” “Life is still beyond your understanding; how would death be within it?”
sentences.n: Ji Lu is Zilu. 鬼神 is a pair: 鬼 the spirits of the dead, the ancestors, and 神 the gods. 未…焉… 'not yet …, how …?': 未 'not yet', and 焉 yān 'how?' asks a question that expects 'you cannot'. 敢問 'I venture to ask' is the polite form of a follow-up question. Zhu Xi: to ask about serving the spirits is to seek the meaning of offering sacrifice, and death is what every man must meet and cannot leave unknown — both are pressing questions; but without the sincerity and reverence to serve men one cannot serve the spirits, and without tracing things to their beginning and knowing how we come to life one cannot follow them to their end and know how we come to die; dark and light, beginning and end are one principle, but learning has an order and steps cannot be skipped, so the Master answered him like this. He quotes Master Cheng: day and night are the Way of death and life; know the Way of life and you know the Way of death; serve men to the full and you serve the spirits to the full — death and life, men and spirits are one and yet two, two and yet one; some say the Master would not tell Zilu, not seeing that this is how he told him most deeply. He Yan's Chen Qun reads it as a refusal: spirits and death are hard to make clear, and talking of them does no good, so he did not answer. Variants: Ruan Yuan's 1816 text and He Yan's have 曰 before 敢問死, marking Zilu's second question as a new speech; He Yan's reads 曰敢問事死 'may I ask about serving the dead?'

sentences.t:
閔子侍側，誾誾如也；
子路，行行如也；
冉有、子貢，侃侃如也。
子樂。

forthright, firm (only in 侃侃, Zhu Xi: 侃苦旦反)

sentences.i: When they were in attendance on him, Master Min was gentle but firm, Zilu all unbending strength, Ran You and Zigong frank and direct. The Master took delight in them.
sentences.n: 侍側 'to attend at the side' of a superior. 閔子 'Master Min' is Min Ziqian — this is the passage Hu Yin had in mind when he guessed that Min's own followers recorded part of the book (11.1). Each description is the X如也 pattern of Book 10: a doubled word, 如 'in the manner of', and 也. 誾誾 and 侃侃 are the words of 10.2 (Zhu Xi: their sound and sense are given in the previous book). 行行 is read hàng hàng (Zhu Xi: 胡浪反), 'the look of hardness and strength' (剛強之貌; He Yan's Zheng Xuan the same). 樂 is lè 'to delight' (Zhu Xi: 音洛). Zhu Xi: he delighted at having gifted men to teach and bring on. Zheng Xuan: he delighted that each was wholly himself. Variants: He Yan's text names 閔子騫 in full and has 冉子 'Master Ran' for 冉有.

sentences.t:
若由也，
不得其死然。
sentences.l:
One like Yóu —
he will not get his proper death.
sentences.i: But a man like Yóu is not going to die in his bed.
sentences.n: 若 'one like, such as'. 由 Yóu is Zilu's personal name, written with its accent to keep it apart from English 'you' (as 2.17). 不得其死 'not to get his death' — not to die the death that is due him, at the end of his years (He Yan's Kong Anguo: 不得以壽終). 然 closes the sentence. Zhu Xi quotes Yin Tun: Zilu was hard and strong, the kind that does not get its proper death, so the Master took the occasion to warn him; and in the end Zilu died in the upheaval of Kong Kui in Wei. He also quotes Hong (洪氏): the Han History quotes this line with 曰 'said' in front of it, and some think the 樂 of 子樂 above is a mistake for 曰 — which would make it 'The Master said: “One like You…”'. The words are the Master's either way, and since they stand past Zhu Xi's comment they are left unquoted.

sentences.t: 魯人為長府。
sentences.l: The men of Lu were working on the Changfu.
sentences.i: The authorities in Lu were rebuilding the Changfu treasury.
sentences.n: 長府 Changfu, 'the Long Storehouse', is a name (Zhu Xi: 藏名, 'the name of a storehouse'; a place for keeping goods and wealth is called 府). 長 is cháng. 為 wéi 'to make, to work on' — Zhu Xi: here, probably, to rebuild it (蓋改作之). He Yan's Zheng Xuan also calls the Changfu a storehouse.

sentences.t:
閔子騫曰：「
仍舊貫，
如之何？
何必改作？」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
what would be wrong with that
to be like, to come up to

sentences.l:
Min Ziqian said: “Going along with the old way —
what about that?
Why must it be changed and remade?”
sentences.i: Min Ziqian said: “What would be wrong with carrying on as before? Why must it be rebuilt?”
sentences.n: 仍 réng is 'to go along with, to keep to' and 貫 is 'the way of doing things' (Zhu Xi: 仍因也，貫事也; He Yan's Zheng Xuan the same). 如之何 'how would it be?' — here a gentle 'what is wrong with that?' 何必 'why must…?' 改作 'to change and make anew'. Zhu Xi quotes a Mr Wang (王氏): rebuilding wears out the people and wastes wealth; where it can be avoided, keeping to the old is better.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
夫人不言，
言必有中。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “That man does not speak;
when he speaks, there is sure to be a hit.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “That man keeps his mouth shut; but when he does say something, it is right on target.”
sentences.n: 夫 is fú 'that' again (Zhu Xi: 音扶), so 夫人 is 'that man', Min Ziqian. 中 is zhòng 'to hit the mark' (Zhu Xi: 去聲), as an arrow hits the target. 有中 'there is a hit'. Zhu Xi: he does not let words out rashly, and when he does they fit principle — only a man of virtue can do this. He Yan's Wang Su: the Master approved of his not wanting to burden the people with rebuilding.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
由之瑟，
奚為於丘之門？」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Yóu's zither —
what is it doing at Qiu's gate?”
sentences.i: The Master said: “What is Yóu's zither-playing doing in my school?”
sentences.n: 瑟 sè is a large zither of many strings. 奚為 'why, for what' — the question word before the verb. 丘 Qiu is the Master's own personal name: he speaks of 'Qiu's gate', his school, as a man names himself modestly. Zhu Xi quotes Master Cheng: the sound of Zilu's playing was not in harmony, not of a piece with the Master's own; and the Kongzi jiayu says Zilu played with the sound of the northern borders, of killing and attack — his temper was hard and bold and fell short of balance and harmony, and so it came out in his music. He Yan's Ma Rong: his playing did not fit the Elegantiae and the Hymns (雅頌). Variant: He Yan's text reads 由之鼓瑟, 'Yóu's playing of the zither'.

sentences.t:
門人不敬子路。
子曰：「
由也升堂矣，
未入於室也。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.i: After that the disciples no longer treated Zilu with respect. The Master said: “Yóu has climbed the steps into the hall; it is only the inner room he has still to enter.”
sentences.n: A house of the time had a raised hall 堂 in front, reached by steps, and the private chamber 室 behind it. 升堂 'going up into the hall' and 入室 'going into the chamber' became a standing figure for stages of learning. 矣 'has already' against 未 'not yet'. Zhu Xi: taking the Master's words, the disciples stopped respecting Zilu, so the Master set it right: going up to the hall and into the chamber are the stages of entering the Way; Zilu's learning had already reached the realm of the correct, the great, the high and the bright — he had only not yet gone deep into what is finest and most hidden — and he must not be slighted for a single failing. He Yan's Ma Rong: the disciples misunderstood, thinking the Master meant to belittle Zilu, so he explained himself.

sentences.t:
子貢問：「
師與商也孰賢？」
子曰：「
師也過，
商也不及。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.i: Zigong asked which was the worthier, Shi or Shang. The Master said: “Shi goes past the mark; Shang stops short of it.”
sentences.n: 師 Shi is Zizhang, Zhuansun Shi; 商 Shang is Zixia, Bu Shang. 與 yǔ 'and' joins the two names, and 也 makes the pair a topic. 孰 'which of the two'. 過 'to go past', 不及 'not to reach'. Zhu Xi: Zizhang had high gifts and wide aims, and liked doing what is difficult for its own sake, so he often went past the mean; Zixia believed firmly and kept carefully, but his compass was narrow, so he often fell short. Variant: He Yan's text reads 孰賢乎.

sentences.t:
曰：「
然則師愈與？」
sentences.l: He said: “If so, then is Shi better?”
sentences.i: “Then Shi is the better of the two?”
sentences.n: 然則 'that being so, then'. 愈 'to surpass, be better' (Zhu Xi: 猶勝也). 與 is yú, the question particle (Zhu Xi: 平聲).

sentences.t:
子曰：「
過猶不及。」
sentences.l: The Master said: “Going past is like not reaching.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Going past the mark misses it just as surely as stopping short of it.”
sentences.n: 猶 'is like, comes to the same as'. Zhu Xi: the Way holds the mean and the constant (中庸) as highest; the excess of the worthy and wise may seem better than the shortfall of the foolish and unworthy, but they miss the mean all the same. He quotes Yin Tun: 'the mean-and-constant as a virtue — is it not the utmost!' (6.27); going too far and not going far enough are equal, and 'miss by a hair and you are a thousand li out'; so the sage's teaching reins in those who go too far and draws on those who fall short, to bring both back to the middle way. He Yan's Kong Anguo: neither hits the mean. Variant: He Yan's text reads 過猶不及也.

sentences.t:
季氏富於周公，
而求也為之聚斂
而附益之。

morph.gloss: Ji, the clan name (Jisun) of the Lu house
clan, house (the family name as a lineage)

sentences.l:
The Ji house was richer than the Duke of Zhou,
and yet Qiu gathered in levies for them
and added still more to it.
sentences.i: The Ji house was richer than the Duke of Zhou had ever been, and yet Qiu squeezed taxes out of the people for them and swelled their wealth further.
sentences.n: 富於周公 'rich beyond the Duke of Zhou': after an adjective, 於 is 'than'. 求 is Ran Qiu, Ran You, then steward of the Ji house (Zhu Xi; He Yan's Kong Anguo). 為之 'for them', 為 wèi (Zhu Xi: 去聲). 聚 'to gather', 斂 'to levy, take in'; 附益 'to add on'. Zhu Xi: the Duke of Zhou was the nearest kin of the royal house, of great merit, holding the office of chief steward, and his wealth was fitting; the Ji were only ministers of a feudal lord, yet richer than he — how could that be, unless they had seized from their ruler and stripped their people? And Ran You, their steward, pressed the taxes still harder to add to it. Kong Anguo: the Duke of Zhou was the Son of Heaven's steward, a minister of the court.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
非吾徒也。
小子鳴鼓而攻之，
可也。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
The Master said: “He is no follower of mine.
Young men, sound the drums and go against him —
that is allowed.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “He is no disciple of mine. You young men have my leave to sound the drums and go after him in the open.”
sentences.n: 徒 'follower, one of a band'. 小子 'young men', the disciples (He Yan's Zheng Xuan: 門人也). 鳴鼓 'to make the drums sound': a public proclamation, as against an offender. 可也 'it is allowed'. Zhu Xi: 'not my follower' cuts him off; sounding the drums and attacking him means having the disciples proclaim his offence and reproach him. The sage hated so much those who side with wrong and harm the people; and yet, since a teacher is stern and friends are close, though he himself cut Ran You off, he still had the disciples set him right — which shows his care for men had no end. He quotes Fan Zuyu: Ran You spent his gift for government on the Ji and so did wrong to this degree; the cause was that his heart was not clear, he did not turn back and look into himself, and was in a hurry to hold office. Zheng Xuan: to sound the drums is to proclaim his offence and reproach him.

sentences.t: 柴也愚，
sentences.l: Chai is foolish,
sentences.i: Chai is not clever,
sentences.n: Four judgments in one shape: a personal name, 也 for the topic, a one-word verdict. Zhu Xi: 柴 Chai is the disciple Gao Chai 高柴, courtesy name Zigao 子羔 (he appears again in 11.24); 愚 here is one whose knowledge falls short but whose solid goodness is more than enough. From the Kongzi jiayu he gives the stories: Gao Chai never stepped on another's shadow, would not kill insects just woken from their winter sleep, would not break off a growing shoot; mourning a parent he wept blood for three years and never once showed his teeth; fleeing danger he would not take a by-path or slip through a hole in a wall — from which one can see what kind of man he was. He Yan's commentary: it is the 'foolishness' of the simple and straight.

sentences.t: 參也魯，
sentences.l: Shen is slow,
sentences.i: Shen is slow,
sentences.n: 參 is Shen, Master Zeng's personal name (read shēn). 魯 'slow, dull' (Zhu Xi: 魯，鈍也; He Yan's Kong Anguo the same). Zhu Xi quotes Master Cheng: Shen got there in the end through his very slowness; Master Zeng's learning was nothing but sincerity and steadiness — among the sage's followers there was no lack of the clever, the gifted and the eloquent, but the one who handed on the Way was the slow man, so in learning sincerity and solidity are what count; and Yin Tun: because his gifts were slow, his learning was sure, and so he could go deep into the Way.

sentences.t: 師也辟，
sentences.l: Shi is all show,
sentences.i: Shi cares too much for appearances,
sentences.n: 師 is Zizhang. 辟 is read pì (Zhu Xi: 婢亦反): Zhu Xi takes it as 便辟, 'practised in deportment and bearing, short on sincerity'. He Yan's text writes the word 僻 'one-sided' and reverses the order, 師僻也; Ma Rong there says Zizhang's gifts surpassed other men's, and his failing lay in being one-sided and glossing over his faults (邪僻文過).

sentences.t: 由也喭。
sentences.l: Yóu is rough.
sentences.i: and Yóu is rough-mannered.
sentences.n: 由 is Zilu. 喭 yàn (Zhu Xi: 五旦反) is 'coarse, unpolished' (粗俗). Zhu Xi quotes Yang Shi: these are four leanings of temperament; the Master told them so that they would know and spur themselves on. He also quotes Wu (吳氏): the words 子曰 'the Master said' have dropped from the start of this chapter — or else the 子曰 at the head of the next chapter belongs here, and the two were one. Variant: He Yan's text reads 由喭也, in the order 'You — rough'.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
回也其庶乎，
屢空。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Hui — he is near, is he not?
Often in want.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Hui has come close, I think — and he is often without a thing.”
sentences.n: 其…乎 'surely … is it not?': a softened judgment. 庶 shù 'near' — Zhu Xi: near to the Way. 屢 lǚ 'often'. 空 is read kòng here, 'empty-handed, in want', the reading classical dictionaries give for this sense (many readers simply say kōng); Zhu Xi glosses it 空匱 'running out' and marks no reading. Zhu Xi: he often came to want, because he would not let poverty move his heart to seek riches; the Master says he is near the Way and also at ease in poverty. He Yan's commentary reads 庶 as 'near to the sage's Way' too, and adds that though often empty-handed he had joy within; it also gives another reading, in which 屢 is 'always' and 空 is 'emptying the heart': only Hui, holding the Way deeply, kept his mind always empty and open.

sentences.t:
賜不受命，
而貨殖焉，
億則屢中。
sentences.i: Ci does not rest content with what Heaven has allotted him: he goes into trade and his wealth grows, and his reckonings about how things will turn out are often right.
sentences.n: The Master's words run on past Zhu Xi's comment and are left unquoted. 賜 Ci is Zigong, Duanmu Ci. 命 here is Heaven's decree, one's lot (Zhu Xi: 命謂天命). 貨殖 'making goods grow': trading for profit; 焉 yān 'with them, by it'. 億 yì 'to estimate, guess' (Zhu Xi: 意度也). 中 zhòng 'to hit the mark' (Zhu Xi: 去聲), as in 11.13. 億則屢中 'guess, and then often hit'. Zhu Xi: Zigong was not, like Yan Hui, at ease in poverty and happy in the Way, but his clear gifts let him judge how affairs would go and often be right. He quotes Master Cheng: Zigong's trading was not the wealth-heaping of later men — only his heart had not let it go; and this was in his youth: once he had heard of human nature and the Way of Heaven (5.12), he no longer did it. And Fan Zuyu: 'often in want' means the basket of rice and gourd of drink often ran out, yet Hui's joy did not change (6.9); nothing in the world could move his heart; wealth and poverty lie with Heaven, and Zigong, setting his mind on trade, could not accept Heaven's decree; his frequent hits were guesses, not a grasp of principle or a contentment with Heaven; the Master once said, 'Unluckily, Ci spoke and was right — that will make him talk the more' — so little did the sage prize talk. He Yan's commentary takes 命 as the Master's instruction (教命), not Heaven's: Ci did not accept his teaching but only grew his goods.

sentences.t:
子張問善人之道。
子曰：「
不踐迹，
亦不入於室。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Zizhang asked about the way of the good man.
The Master said: “He does not tread in the footprints,
and also he does not enter the chamber.”
sentences.i: Zizhang asked what the good man's way was. The Master said: “He does not walk in the tracks others have left — but neither does he get into the inner room.”
sentences.n: 善人 'the good man' ranks, in the Analects, below the sage and the gentleman (7.25). 道 dào here is 'way, course'. 踐 jiàn 'to tread', 迹 jì 'footprints, tracks'. 亦 'also, but also'. 室 'the inner chamber', the figure of 11.14. Zhu Xi: the good man has fine natural stuff but has not learned. He quotes Master Cheng: 踐迹 is like 'keeping to the road and the wheel-ruts'; the good man, though he does not need to tread in the old tracks, does no evil of himself, but neither can he enter the sage's chamber. And Zhang Zai: the good man wants humaneness but has not set his will on learning; because he wants humaneness, though he does not walk by the established models he does not step into evil — the good is his own; because he does not learn, he has no way in to the sage's chamber. He Yan's Kong Anguo: 踐 is 'to follow'; the good man does not merely follow old tracks — he can create something of his own — but he does not reach the sage's inner room.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
論篤是與，
君子者乎？
色莊者乎？」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
The Master said: “Earnest talk — this we approve:
is he a gentleman?
Or one grave in his looks?”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Suppose we give a man our approval for the earnestness of his talk: is he a gentleman, or just a man with a solemn face?”
sentences.n: 論篤是與 shows the object put first and picked up by 是 'this': 'earnest talk — this (we) approve', that is, 與論篤 'approve of earnest talk'. 與 is yǔ 'to side with, approve' (Zhu Xi: 而與之, 'and approve of him'). 論 lùn 'talk, what a man says'; 篤 'solid, earnest'. 莊 zhuāng 'grave, dignified'. The two questions with 乎 set the alternatives side by side. Zhu Xi: if we approve of a man only because his talk is solid and earnest, we do not know whether he is a gentleman or someone grave only in his looks — one must not judge men by words and looks. He Yan's commentary reads it quite differently, as three kinds of men, all praised: one earnest in talk (with no careless word in his mouth), the gentleman (with no mean act in his conduct), and one grave in his looks (stern without malice, keeping petty men at a distance) — all three can count as good men, which links the line to 11.19 before it.

sentences.t:
子路問：「聞斯行諸？」
子曰：「
有父兄在，
如之何其聞斯行之？」
冉有問：「聞斯行諸？」
子曰：「聞斯行之。」
公西華曰：「
由也問『聞斯行諸』，
子曰『有父兄在』；
求也問『聞斯行諸』，
子曰『聞斯行之』。
赤也惑，
敢問。」
子曰：「
求也退，
故進之；
由也兼人，
故退之。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
Ran You — the disciple Ran Qiu
Ran, a surname (Ran You, Ran Qiu)
Gongxi Hua — the disciple Gongxi Chi
doubles, does the part of two

sentences.l:
Zilu asked: “Hearing something, should one straightway do it?”
The Master said:
“There are father and elder brothers living —
how could you, hearing, straightway do it?”
Ran You asked: “Hearing something, should one straightway do it?”
The Master said: “Hearing it, straightway do it.”
Gongxi Hua said:
“Yóu asked, ‘Hearing something, should one straightway do it?’
and you said, ‘There are father and elder brothers living’;
Qiu asked, ‘Hearing something, should one straightway do it?’
and you said, ‘Hearing it, straightway do it.’
Chi is perplexed,
and ventures to ask.”
The Master said:
“Qiu draws back,
so I moved him forward;
Yóu does the part of two men,
so I drew him back.”
sentences.i: Zilu asked whether he should put a thing into practice the moment he heard it. The Master said: “Your father and elder brothers are still alive — how can you go ahead as soon as you hear?” Ran You asked the same question. The Master said: “Yes: what you hear, carry out at once.” Gongxi Hua said: “When Yóu asked, you reminded him that his father and elder brothers were alive. When Qiu asked, you told him to carry it out at once. I am puzzled, and venture to ask why.” The Master said: “Qiu is timid, so I gave him a push. Yóu is out to outdo everyone, so I put a check on him.”
sentences.n: Three disciples, each under two names: 子路 Zilu is Zhong You 仲由, whom the Master calls 由 Yóu; 冉有 Ran You is Ran Qiu 冉求, called 求 Qiu; 公西華 Gongxi Hua is Gongxi Chi 公西赤, who names himself 赤 Chi. The narrative uses the courtesy name, speech the personal name. 聞斯行諸 is a whole question in four characters: 斯 'then, straightway' ties the doing to the hearing, and the final 諸 is the fused 之乎 'it?'. 如之何其… 'how could…?', with 其 softening the verb. 進 'to advance' and 退 'to draw back' are used causatively: 進之 'I moved him forward', 退之 'I held him back'. 兼人 is literally 'to double a man'; Zhu Xi: 兼人謂勝人也, 'to outdo others'. Zhu Xi quotes Zhang Jingfu (Zhang Shi): on hearing what is right one should certainly be bold to do it, but while father and elder brothers live there are things one may not decide alone, and to act without taking their orders would itself harm what is right; Zilu, who feared to hear more before he had acted on what he had heard (5.13), was in no danger of failing to act — the danger was that he would overdo it and skip what needs their word; Ran Qiu's endowment erred toward weakness, and the danger was that he would hesitate and shrink from what he ought to do; the sage pushed one forward and held the other back to bring both within what is right, with neither excess nor shortfall. He Yan's Bao Xian takes the thing heard to be relief of the destitute; Kong Anguo: one should tell father and elder brothers and may not decide alone; Zheng Xuan: Ran You was modest and retiring by nature, Zilu bent on outdoing others, and each was corrected where he went wrong. Variant: He Yan's text ends the Master's first answer 如之何其聞斯行之也, with a final particle.

sentences.t:
子畏於匡，
顔淵後。
子曰：「吾以女為死矣。」
曰：「子在，
回何敢死？」

morph.gloss: was in danger, on his guard
= 顏 (the edition's form): Yan (a surname, in 顔淵)
Yuan (in 顏淵, from the courtesy name Ziyuan)

sentences.l:
The Master was in danger at Kuang, and Yan Yuan fell behind.
The Master said: “I took you for dead.”
He said: “While you, Master, live,
how would Hui dare to die?”
sentences.i: When the Master was in danger at Kuang, Yan Yuan was separated from him and caught up only later. The Master said: “I thought you had been killed.” He said: “As long as you are alive, Master, how could I let myself die?”
sentences.n: 畏於匡 as at 9.5: 畏 wèi is here 'to be in danger, on one's guard', and Kuang the place where the people took the Master for Yang Hu and surrounded him. 後 'came behind': Zhu Xi, they lost each other and he was left behind; He Yan's Kong Anguo says the same. 女 is rǔ 'you' (Zhu Xi: 女音汝). 以 A 為 B 'to take A as B': 以女為死 'took you as dead'. In the answer 子 is 'you, Master', and Yan Yuan calls himself by his personal name, 回 Hui. 何敢死: Zhu Xi, he would not rush into the fight and get himself killed. He quotes Hu Yin at length: under the former kings' order a man lives by three — father, teacher and lord — serves them as one, and dies wherever his duty lies; between Yan Yuan and the Master both kindness and duty were complete, more than between ordinary teacher and pupil; had the Master met disaster, Hui would have thrown away his life to go to him, and had he himself survived he would have appealed to the Son of Heaven above and the regional lord below for a punitive expedition to avenge him; but with the Master alive, why would he not hold his life dear rather than run on the blades of the men of Kuang? He Yan's Bao Xian: with the Master alive, there was nothing for which he might dare to die.

sentences.t: 季子然問：「仲由、冉求可謂大臣與？」

morph.gloss: Ji Ziran — a younger member of the Ji house
Zhong, the courtesy name of Guan Yiwu
Ran, a surname (Ran You, Ran Qiu)

sentences.l: Ji Ziran asked: “Zhong You and Ran Qiu — can they be called great ministers?”
sentences.i: Ji Ziran asked whether Zhong You and Ran Qiu could be called great ministers.
sentences.n: 季子然 Ji Ziran: Zhu Xi, a younger member of the Ji house (季氏子弟), proud that his family had got these two as its ministers, and so he asked; He Yan's Kong Anguo says the same. 仲由 is Zilu and 冉求 Ran You, here under family and personal names; both were then in the Ji's service (Zhu Xi has Ran You as the Ji's steward at 3.6 and Zilu at 11.24). 可謂 'can be called'. 與 is yú, the question particle (Zhu Xi: 平聲). 大臣 'a great minister' is a minister great in worth, not merely in rank; the Master defines it two units on.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
吾以子為異之問，
曾由與求之問。」

morph.gloss: and it turns out, after all

sentences.i: The Master said: “I thought you were going to ask me about someone out of the common run, and it is only Yóu and Qiu.”
sentences.n: 異之問 and 由與求之問 are both fronted objects marked by 之: not 問異 'ask about the unusual' but 異之問, and not 問由與求 but 由與求之問 — the object is put first for weight and 之 holds its place. 子 here is 'you, sir', polite address to the questioner. 曾 is zēng, 'and it turns out' (Zhu Xi: 曾猶乃也), as in 3.6. 與 yǔ 'and'. Zhu Xi: 異 is 'out of the ordinary'; the Master makes light of the two in order to take Ji Ziran down. He Yan's Kong Anguo: 'I thought you were asking about something unusual — and it is these two; how could they amount to great ministers?'

sentences.t:
所謂大臣者，
以道事君，
不可則止。
sentences.l:
What is called a great minister
serves his lord by the Way,
and when that cannot be, he stops.
sentences.i: A true great minister serves his lord by the Way; when the Way cannot be followed, he steps down.
sentences.n: The Master's reply runs on past Zhu Xi's comment here and in the next unit, and is left unquoted. 所謂…者 'what is called…': the opening of a definition. 以道事君 'serves his lord by means of the Way': 以 'by', 事 'to serve'. 不可則止 'not possible, then stop': the 則 'then' joins condition and consequence with no 'if'. Zhu Xi: 以道事君 means he does not go along with his lord's desires; 不可則止 means he is sure to carry out his own resolve (必行己之志).

sentences.t:
今由與求也，
可謂具臣矣。

morph.gloss: ministers who fill out the number

sentences.l:
Now Yóu and Qiu
can be called ministers who fill out the number.
sentences.i: As for Yóu and Qiu, they fill out the number of ministers, and that is all.
sentences.n: 具臣: Zhu Xi, 具臣謂備臣數而已, 'ministers who complete the number of ministers, and no more'; He Yan's Kong Anguo has the same words. 具 is 'to be provided, to fill out'. 也 after 由與求 marks them as the topic. The Master's answer closes here.

sentences.t: 曰：「然則從之者與？」
sentences.l: He said: “Then are they men who follow him?”
sentences.i: “Then,” he said, “they will simply do as they are told?”
sentences.n: The speaker is Ji Ziran again. 然則 'that being so, then'. 從之者 'those who follow him': 之, Zhu Xi says, is the Ji — if the two are not great ministers, they will just go along with whatever the Ji do. 與 yú is the question particle (Zhu Xi: 平聲). He Yan's Kong Anguo takes the question more generally: is a minister then always to follow his lord's wishes?

sentences.t:
子曰：「弑父與君，
亦不從也。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “To murder a father or a lord —
that even so they would not follow.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “If it came to killing a father or a lord, they would not go along with that.”
sentences.n: 弑 is the killing of a superior: a subject's murder of his lord, a son's of his father. 與 yǔ 'and, or'. 亦 'even so, all the same'. Zhu Xi: the two fall short of the way of a great minister, but they have learned thoroughly what is due between lord and minister, and in the greatest crime of all they would certainly not follow; the Master is crediting them with a loyalty that would die in a crisis and could not be taken from them, and at the same time quietly breaking the Ji's ambition to be no one's subject. He quotes Yin Tun: the Ji held power and usurped what was not theirs; the two served in their house and could not set it right, knew it was wrong and could not stop it — 'ministers who fill out the number' indeed; at that time the Ji already thought of doing without their duke, boasted of the men they had got, and supposed they could make them follow; hence 'murdering a father or a lord they would not follow' — and so the two might be spared. He Yan's Kong Anguo: though the two follow their master, they would not join him in great treason.

sentences.t: 子路使子羔為費宰。

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l: Zilu had Zigao made steward of Bi.
sentences.i: Zilu got Zigao appointed steward of Bi.
sentences.n: 子羔 Zigao is Gao Chai 高柴, the Chai of 11.17 (Zhu Xi there: 姓高字子羔). 使 'to cause, to have (someone) do'; 為 wéi 'to act as'. 費 Bi, read bì (Zhu Xi at 6.7: 音秘), was a town of the Ji house, the stewardship Min Ziqian refused (6.7). Zhu Xi: Zilu was then steward of the Ji and put Zigao forward.

sentences.t: 子曰：「賊夫人之子。」
sentences.l: The Master said: “You are doing harm to that man's son.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “You will be the ruin of the young man.”
sentences.n: 賊 is 'to harm, to injure' (Zhu Xi: 賊害也). 夫 is fú 'that' (Zhu Xi: 夫音扶, and so below): 夫人之子 is 'that man's son', the young Zigao — not 夫人 fū rén 'a lady'. Zhu Xi: Zigao's nature was fine but he had not yet learned; to set him at once to governing people would only harm him. He Yan's Bao Xian: his learning was not yet well practised, and to make him govern was to do him harm.

sentences.t:
子路曰：「
有民人焉，
有社稷焉，
何必讀書，
然後為學？」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the altars of soil and grain

sentences.l:
Zilu said:
“There are people there;
there are the altars of soil and grain there:
why must one read books,
and only then count it as learning?”
sentences.i: Zilu said: “He will have people to govern and the altars of soil and grain to tend. Why must a man read books before what he does can be called learning?”
sentences.n: 焉 is the fused 於是 'in it, there': in Bi there are people to rule and spirits to serve. 社稷 are the altars of the god of the soil and of the god of grain, whose sacrifices stood for the life of a state or domain. 然後 'only after that'; 為學 'to count as learning', 為 wéi. Zhu Xi: governing people and serving the spirits are both ways of learning — so Zilu argues. He Yan's Kong Anguo puts it the same way: to practise in governing people and serving the spirits is also learning.

sentences.t: 子曰：「是故惡夫佞者。」
sentences.l: The Master said: “This is why I detest the glib.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “This is just why I cannot stand a man with a ready tongue.”
sentences.n: 是故 'for this reason'. 惡 is wù 'to hate' (Zhu Xi: 去聲), 夫 fú 'those' (音扶). 佞 'glib', as in 5.5. Zhu Xi: governing people and serving spirits are certainly a learner's business, but only when learning is complete should one take office and put it into practice; set a man who has never learned in office to learn by it, and he will hardly fail to slight the spirits and oppress the people. Zilu did not mean what he said: his case was beaten and his words exhausted, so he fell back on his tongue to fend the Master off — which is why the Master did not rebut the argument but only showed his dislike of the glibness. He quotes Fan Zuyu: in antiquity men learned first and then entered government — no one heard of learning by governing; the root of the Way is cultivating oneself, and only then does it reach to governing others; the account of it is in the books, and one reads and knows before one can act — how can one not read? Zilu would have Zigao learn through government, losing the order of first and last, root and branch; not knowing his error, he fended others off with a ready tongue, so the Master detested his glibness. He Yan's Kong Anguo: he disliked a man who used a quick tongue to push through his own wrong without knowing when he was beaten.

sentences.t: 子路、曾晳、冉有、公西華侍坐。

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
Zeng Xi — the disciple Zeng Dian, Master Zeng's father
Ran, a surname (Ran You, Ran Qiu)

sentences.l: Zilu, Zeng Xi, Ran You and Gongxi Hua sat in attendance.
sentences.i: Zilu, Zeng Xi, Ran You and Gongxi Hua were sitting with the Master.
sentences.n: The longest exchange in Book 11, running over twelve units. 曾晳 Zeng Xi is Zeng Dian 曾點 (the edition prints 㸃), father of Master Zeng, Zeng Shen (Zhu Xi: 晳曾參父名㸃; He Yan's Kong Anguo the same). 侍坐 'to sit in attendance' on a superior; Zhu Xi marks 坐 才卧反, which is modern zuò in any case. The four sat, Zhu Xi says later (unit 56), in order of age.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
以吾一日長乎爾，
毋吾以也。」
sentences.l:
The Master said:
“Because I am a day older than you —
do not hold back on my account.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “I may be a little older than you, but don't let that keep you from speaking.”
sentences.n: 長 is zhǎng 'older, senior' (Zhu Xi: 上聲). 乎 is the comparative 'than' (= 於). 一日 'one day' is a modest way of saying 'a little'. 毋吾以 shows the rule for pronoun objects in negative sentences: 毋以吾 'do not, because of me' becomes 毋吾以, the pronoun before the verb (as 未之有 in 1.2). Zhu Xi: 'though I am somewhat older than you, do not find it hard to speak because of that' — the Master is drawing them out to say all they think, so he can see their aims, and Zhu Xi finds the sage's warmth and humility in it. He Yan's Kong Anguo: 'I am asking you: do not find it hard to answer because I am older.' The speech runs on into the next unit, where it is left unquoted.

sentences.t:
居則曰「不吾知也！」
如或知爾，
則何以哉？
sentences.l:
In everyday life you say, “No one knows me!”
If someone did know you,
then what would you do?
sentences.i: You are forever saying, “Nobody recognises what I am worth.” Suppose someone did — what would you have to offer?
sentences.n: The Master is still speaking. 居 'dwelling, in ordinary times' — Zhu Xi: 平居, day in, day out. 不吾知 is another fronted pronoun in a negative sentence: 不知吾 becomes 不吾知 'not me knows'. 知 zhī, 'to know, to recognise (a man's worth)', as in 1.1, 1.16 and 4.14. 何以 'with what?' — Zhu Xi: if someone knew you, what would you be of use for? He Yan's Kong Anguo: 'if someone employed you, how would you govern?'

sentences.t:
子路率爾而對曰：「
千乘之國，
攝乎大國之閒，
加之以師旅，
因之以饑饉，
由也為之，
比及三年，
可使有勇，
且知方也。」
夫子哂之。

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Zilu, all in a hurry, answered, saying:
“A state of a thousand chariots,
hemmed in between great states,
with armies laid upon it
and famine following on —
let Yóu manage it,
and by the time three years came round
I could give them courage,
and make them know which way to face.”
The Master smiled faintly at him.
sentences.i: Zilu was quick to answer, and spoke first: “Give me a state of a thousand chariots wedged between great powers, with armies bearing down on it and famine on top of that. If I had charge of it, within three years I could put courage into its people and set them facing toward what is right.” The Master gave a slight smile.
sentences.n: 率爾 shuài ěr: Zhu Xi, 'hasty, abrupt' (輕遽之貌); 爾 makes a description as 然 does. He Yan's commentary: he answered before the other three — ahead of his turn. 千乘之國 is the 'state of a thousand chariots' of 1.5 (乘 shèng; Zhu Xi: 去聲). 攝 shè: Zhu Xi, 'held in check, hemmed in' (管束也); Bao Xian, 'pressed' (攝迫). 閒 jiān 'the space between'. 加之以 X 'add X to it', 因之以 Y 'follow it up with Y': 以 marks the thing added, and Zhu Xi glosses 因 as 仍 'and again on top'. 師旅 are armies — Zhu Xi: 2,500 men make a 師, 500 a 旅. 饑饉 jī jǐn (Zhu Xi: 饑音機, 饉音僅): grain failing is 饑, vegetables failing 饉. 由也為之 'Yóu managing it': Zilu names himself; 為 wéi. 比及 'by the time it comes to': Zhu Xi marks 比 必二反, bì, the traditional reading for this word, kept here (some modern readers say bǐ). 方 Zhu Xi glosses as 向 'direction': facing toward what is right; a people that does will hold close to its superiors and die for its leaders. 哂 shěn is a faint smile (Zhu Xi: 微笑也); He Yan's Ma Rong just 'laughed'. Why the Master smiled is asked in unit 58. Variant: He Yan's text reads 攝乎大國間, without 之.

sentences.t:
求！爾何如？
對曰：「
方六七十，
如五六十，
求也為之，
比及三年，
可使足民。
如其禮樂，
以俟君子。」

morph.gloss: to be like, to come up to
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
“Qiu, what of you?”
He answered:
“A place sixty or seventy li square,
or fifty or sixty —
let Qiu manage it,
and by the time three years came round
I could see the people have enough.
As for its rites and music,
for those I would wait for a gentleman.”
sentences.i: “Qiu, what about you?” He answered: “A territory sixty or seventy li across, or say fifty or sixty: if I had charge of it, within three years I could see that the people had all they needed. The rites and music would have to wait for a gentleman.”
sentences.n: The Master's question has no 子曰: Zhu Xi notes that 求爾何如 is Confucius asking, and so with the questions below. 爾 'you'. 方六七十 'sixty or seventy (li) square': 方 is 'square, on each side', and the li (a measure of distance, well under a mile) is understood. Zhu Xi: a small state; 如 is 或 'or', and fifty or sixty is smaller still. 足 'to have enough' — Zhu Xi: 富足, well provided. 如其禮樂 'as for its rites and music' (樂 yuè); 俟 'to wait for'. Zhu Xi: 'wait for a gentleman' says it is beyond him; Ran You was modest and retiring, and, having seen Zilu smiled at, made his words humbler still. He Yan's Kong Anguo: he claims only to make the people's clothing and food sufficient; transforming them by rites and music must wait for a gentleman — words of modesty. Variant: He Yan's text reads 可使足民也, with a final particle.

sentences.t:
赤！爾何如？
對曰：「
非曰能之，
願學焉。
宗廟之事，
如㑹同，
端章甫，
願為小相焉。」

morph.gloss: to be like, to come up to
(and) the zhangfu cap — a ceremonial cap

sentences.l:
“Chi, what of you?”
He answered:
“I do not say I can do it;
I wish to learn it.
At the business of the ancestral temple,
or at the lords' gatherings at court,
in black robe and zhangfu cap,
I would wish to serve as a minor assistant.”
sentences.i: “Chi, what about you?” He answered: “It isn't that I can do this already — I want to learn it. At the sacrifices in the ancestral temple, or when the lords meet at court, I should like to stand by in black robe and ceremonial cap as a junior assistant.”
sentences.n: Zhu Xi: Gongxi Hua's heart was set on the rites and music, and not wanting to seem to put himself in the gentleman's place, he opened with modest words — not that he could, only that he wished to learn. 焉 'in it, there'. 宗廟之事 is the sacrifices in the ancestral temple. 㑹同 (㑹 is the edition's form of 會 huì): Zhu Xi, when the lords appear at court as occasion arises it is called 會, when they all come together it is 同. 端 is the black court robe (玄端服), 章甫 a ceremonial cap (禮冠). 相 is xiàng 'one who assists the lord at the rites' (Zhu Xi: 去聲; 相贊君之禮者); 'minor' is modesty too. 為 wéi 'to serve as'. He Yan's Zheng Xuan gives the same account of the audiences and dress, the robe and cap a lord wore to hold court. Variant: He Yan's text reads 非曰能之也, with a final particle.

sentences.t:
㸃！爾何如？
鼓瑟希，
鏗爾，
舍瑟而作，
對曰：「異乎三子者之撰。」
子曰：「何傷乎？
亦各言其志也。」
曰：「
莫春者，
春服旣成，
冠者五六人，
童子六七人，
浴乎沂，
風乎舞雩，
詠而歸。」
夫子喟然歎曰：「吾與㸃也！」

morph.gloss: to be like, to come up to
setting-out — what they have laid out
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
“Dian, what of you?”
His zither playing thinned out;
then, with a twang,
he put the zither down and rose,
and answered: “Mine differs from what the three gentlemen have laid out.”
The Master said: “What harm is there?
Each is only telling his aims.”
He said:
“Late in spring,
the spring clothes made,
with five or six capped young men
and six or seven boys,
to wash in the Yi,
catch the breeze at the rain-dance terrace,
and chant on the way home.”
The Master sighed heavily and said: “I side with Dian!”
sentences.i: “Dian, what about you?” The notes of his zither grew sparse; he let it fall still with a last twang, set it aside and rose. “My wish is not like what these three have offered,” he answered. “What harm in that?” said the Master. “Each is only saying where his heart is set.” He said: “At the end of spring, when the spring clothes are ready, I would go with five or six young men who have been capped and six or seven boys, wash in the river Yi, stand in the wind at the rain-dance terrace, and come back with a song.” The Master drew a long sigh and said: “Dian's wish is my own.”
sentences.n: 㸃 is the edition's form of 點 Dian, Zeng Xi's personal name. Readings, all Zhu Xi's: 鏗 kēng (苦耕反), 舍 shě 'to put down' (上聲), 撰 zhuàn (士免反), 莫 mù and 冠 guàn (並去聲), 沂 yí (漁依反), 雩 yú (音于). Zhu Xi: they sat in order of age, so Dian should have answered next after Zilu, but he was playing the zither, so the Master asked Qiu and Chi first. 希 is the playing slowing and pausing; 作 'to rise'; 撰 'what one sets out, one's provision' (具也). 莫春 is late spring (莫 = 暮), the mild warm season; 春服 are unlined and lined spring garments; 冠者 young men who have been capped, i.e. come of age, against 童子 'boys'. 浴 is washing, like the purification by water on the first si-day of the third month in Zhu Xi's own day; the Yi is a river south of the city of Lu, said by the geographical treatise (地志) to have warm springs, which Zhu Xi thinks likely. 風 is 'to take the cool air'; 舞雩 the place of the sacrifice to Heaven praying for rain, with an altar, a levelled ground and trees; 詠 is singing. 吾與㸃 'I side with Dian': 與 yǔ is 'to approve' (as 5.8 吾與女). Zhu Xi reads the whole as Dian's having seen that where selfish desire is spent the principle of Heaven flows through everything, filling every place with nothing lacking; so he was at ease in action and in rest, and his aim was only to take the place he stood in and enjoy the common round of days, with no thought of putting himself aside to serve others; his heart moved freely with heaven and earth and all things, each in its place, and this showed silently beyond his words — beside it the three, intent on the details of affairs, were of another stature, and so the Master sighed and approved him deeply. He Yan's Bao Xian reads the scene more plainly: late spring is the third month, when unlined and lined clothes are worn; 'I would like to get five or six capped men and six or seven boys, wash at the waters of the Yi, take the cool below the rain-dance terrace, sing the Way of the former kings, and come home to the Master's gate'; Zhou Shenglie: the Master approved Dian for alone knowing the season. Variants: He Yan's text writes 暮春, the word Zhu Xi reads 莫 as, and 得冠者五六人 'to get five or six capped young men', as Bao Xian paraphrases.

sentences.t:
三子者出，
曾晳後。
曾晳曰：「夫三子者之言何如？」
子曰：「亦各言其志也已矣。」

morph.gloss: to be like, to come up to

sentences.l:
The three went out; Zeng Xi stayed behind.
Zeng Xi said: “The words of those three — what of them?”
The Master said: “Each was only telling his aims, and that is all.”
sentences.i: The other three went out, and Zeng Xi stayed behind. “What did you think of what those three said?” he asked. The Master said: “Each was simply saying what he had set his heart on, nothing more.”
sentences.n: 三子者 'the three gentlemen'. 後 'came after, stayed behind'. 夫 is fú 'those' (Zhu Xi: 音扶). 也已矣 stacks three final particles: 'and that is all, and so it is' — the Master repeats his answer of unit 56 and closes the matter.

sentences.t: 曰：「夫子何哂由也？」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l: He said: “Master, why did you smile at Yóu?”
sentences.i: “Master, why did you smile at Yóu?” he asked.
sentences.n: Zeng Xi is the speaker; 夫子 'Master', here in address. Zhu Xi: Dian thought Zilu's aim was something he was well able to do, yet the Master smiled at it, so he asked the reason.

sentences.t:
曰：「
為國以禮，
其言不讓，
是故哂之。」
sentences.l:
He said:
“Governing a state is by the rites;
his words did not give way —
this is why I smiled at him.”
sentences.i: He said: “A state is governed by the rites, and his words had no deference in them. That is why I smiled.”
sentences.n: The speaker is now the Master. 為國 'to govern a state', 為 wéi. 以禮 'by means of the rites'. 讓 is 'to yield, to give way, deference' — the spirit of the rites (as 4.13 能以禮讓為國). 是故 'for this reason'. Zhu Xi: the Master granted his ability; he smiled only at his want of modesty. He Yan's Bao Xian: governing a state is by the rites, and the rites prize deference; Zilu's words did not defer, so he laughed. Master Cheng's comment on this (quoted at unit 61): Zilu failed only to grasp the principle of governing by the rites; had he grasped it, his would have been Dian's bearing too. Variant: He Yan's text opens 子曰為國以禮, naming the Master as speaker.

sentences.t:
唯求則非邦也與？
安見方六七十，
如五六十，
而非邦也者？
sentences.l:
“But Qiu — was it not a state?”
“Where would one see sixty or seventy li square,
or fifty or sixty,
that is not a state?”
sentences.i: Zeng Xi asked: “And Qiu — wasn't it a state that he was talking about?” The Master said: “Where have you ever seen a territory sixty or seventy li across, or fifty or sixty, that was not a state?”
sentences.n: No 曰 marks the change of speaker. Zhu Xi reads the first line as Zeng Xi's question and the second as the Master's reply: Dian, seeing that Qiu also wished to govern a state and was not smiled at, quietly asked; the Master's answer has no word of blame, so he approves Qiu too. The lines can also be taken as the Master's own continuing reply; we follow Zhu Xi. 唯 wéi 'but, as for'. 與 is yú, the question particle (Zhu Xi: 平聲, and so in the next unit). 安見…者 'where would one see one that…?', a rhetorical question: 安 'where, how', and 者 closes the description, 'such a one as is not a state'. 方 'square' and 如 'or', as in unit 54.

sentences.t:
唯赤則非邦也與？
宗廟㑹同，
非諸侯而何？
赤也為之小，
孰能為之大？

morph.gloss: to take as chief, to look up to as head (Zhu Xi: 主)
to meet, a meeting of the feudal lords (㑹同, 11.25

sentences.l:
“But Chi — was it not a state?”
“The ancestral temple and the gatherings at court —
if not the lords' business, what are they?
If Chi were the small one in them,
who could be the great?”
sentences.i: “And Chi — wasn't it a state with him too?” “Sacrifices in the ancestral temple and audiences at court — what are they if not the business of lords? If Chi is to be the junior there, who could be the senior?”
sentences.n: Again, Zhu Xi says, Zeng Xi asks and the Master answers. 非諸侯而何 'not the lords — then what?': 而 joins the condition to the question. 赤也為之小 'Chi being small in them'; 孰能為之大 'who could be great in them?' — 為 wéi 'to be'. Zhu Xi: no one could surpass him; these too are words of approval. He Yan's Kong Anguo: all of these are lords' affairs, as Zilu's was; the Master laughed at Zilu only for not deferring. Zhu Xi closes the passage with Master Cheng's comments: the learners of old were steady and well nourished and kept an order of first and last — Zilu, Ran You and Gongxi Chi spoke of real affairs, and the Master approved them; later learners love the lofty, their minds roaming a thousand li off while their bodies stay here. And: the Master approved Dian because Dian's aim was one with the sage's — the bearing of Yao and Shun; he truly differed from the three, only his conduct did not make good his words, which is what is meant by 'wild' (狂); the others saw small things; Zilu only failed to grasp the principle of governing by the rites, and had he grasped it, his would have been this bearing too. And: the three all wanted a state to govern, so the Master did not choose them; Dian, a 'wild' one, could not necessarily do the work of a sage, but could know the Master's aim — washing in the Yi and coming home chanting is joy, and each thing finding its place; the Master's aim was that the old should have ease, friends good faith and the young care (5.25), and that all things should fulfil their nature, and Dian knew it. And: Zeng Dian and Qidiao Kai had already seen the great meaning. Variants: He Yan's text reads 宗廟之事如會同, as in unit 55; 非諸侯如之何 'if not lords, what is it?'; and 孰能為之大相 'who could be its great assistant?', which Kong Anguo explains: Chi modestly says a minor assistant — who then could be a great one?
